name: Bauhaus
basis: a design school's conventions: tiles swapped for primary shapes and colours by brightness (how)

lumenary.blurb: The picture reduced to circles, quarter-circles and squares in primary colours.

facts.bestOn: Bold scenes with a clear subject and simple shapes

why: The Bauhaus school wanted design to start from the plainest forms: square, circle, triangle, and the primary colours. This treatment applies that idea to a photograph. Each tile of the picture is swapped for one simple shape, and tone is told by how much of the tile the shape fills, so a dark patch is a solid square and a bright one is a small dot.
how: Cut the picture into a grid of square tiles.
Measure the average brightness of each tile.
Pick a shape from brightness: square, quarter circle, half circle, circle or dot, from darkest to lightest.
Pick a colour from the tile’s hue: red, yellow or blue, with black and paper for the extremes.
Turn each curved shape to follow the nearest edge in the picture.
history: Walter Gropius founded the Bauhaus in Weimar in 1919. It moved to Dessau in 1925 and to Berlin in 1932, and it closed in 1933 under political pressure. Teachers such as Wassily Kandinsky, Paul Klee, László Moholy-Nagy and Josef Albers shaped its ideas about form and colour. Kandinsky is remembered for asking which colour belongs to which basic shape, and his answer, yellow triangle, red square, blue circle, still echoes in posters today.
uses: Brand identity systems built from a few shapes
terms: Red, yellow and blue, the three from which painters traditionally mix the rest.
A quarter of a disc, drawn in one corner of a tile. Four orientations are possible.
To snap a smooth value, such as an edge direction, to one of a few allowed choices.
paragraphs: The picture is cut into square tiles, and each tile is replaced by one geometric shape, as in a Bauhaus poster. The shape depends on brightness in five bands: darkest tiles become full squares, then quarter circles, half circles, circles, and the lightest a small dot, so tone is carried by how much of the tile the shape fills. The colour depends on hue: reds become red, yellows and greens become yellow, everything else blue; very dark tiles are black, and low-saturation tiles are black, paper or blue by brightness.

The orientation of a quarter or half circle follows the picture’s own edges. The Sobel gradient at the tile gives a direction, and that direction is quantised into one of four quadrants, so the curves lean along contours. The variation slider reassigns some tiles at random using a generator seeded from the tile’s index and the seed, so “Shuffle” gives another reproducible design and the same seed always gives the same poster.

equations.note: Quarter-turn orientation from the edge direction at the tile.

presets.text: Use more tiles for a sharper portrait, in a single colour family.
Go coarse for a bold, almost abstract poster in dusk colours.
Set variation to zero to see the pure rule with no random swaps.
